title: Visual symbolic mechanisms: Emergent symbol processing in Vision Language Models
claim: Model binding is supported by a staged, content-independent position-ID mechanism, and converging representational and causal analyses reveal each stage in different layers.
layout: 4 panels in a 2x2 grid: (a) architecture diagram top-left, (b) PCA scatter bottom-left, (c) line plot top-right, (d) heatmap bottom-right; panel labels below each
description: A four-panel figure. Panel (a) is a flow diagram. A scene with an orange triangle (ID=0) and a purple triangle (ID=1) sits at the top left. Three colored boxes are labeled ID Retrieval Heads (blue), ID Selection Heads (red) and Feature Retrieval Heads (green). Solid arrows show feedforward flow and dashed arrows show attention. The prompt text "There is an orange triangle and a" runs along the bottom, and the output "purple triangle" is at the top. Panel (b) shows PCA scatter clusters at layers 19 and 27. Rows are colored by target position and by target features, with legends on the right. Panel (c) is a line plot of correlation against layer, with blue, red and green curves peaking at different layers. Panel (d) is a black heatmap of layer index against head index. A few bright blue, red and green squares mark the three stages.
caption: Overview of position ID architecture and supporting evidence. We identify three processing stages: ID retrieval heads that retrieve the position ID of objects described in the prompt, ID selection heads that select the position ID for a target object, and feature retrieval heads that use this position ID to retrieve the features of the target object. These stages are revealed both by (b,c) representational and (d) causal mediation analyses (see text for explanation).
abstract: To accurately process a visual scene, observers must bind features together to represent individual objects. This capacity is necessary, for instance, to distinguish an image containing a red square and a blue circle from an image containing a blue square and a red circle. Recent work has found that language models solve this 'binding problem' via a set of symbol-like, content-independent indices, but it is unclear whether similar mechanisms are employed by Vision Language Models (VLMs). This question is especially relevant, given the persistent failures of VLMs on tasks that require binding. Here, we identify a previously unknown set of emergent symbolic mechanisms that support binding specifically in VLMs, via a content-independent, spatial indexing scheme. Moreover, we find that binding errors, when they occur, can be traced directly to failures in these mechanisms. Taken together, these results shed light on the mechanisms that support symbol-like processing in VLMs, and suggest possible avenues for reducing the number of binding failures exhibited by these models.
